questions.stem: Under which Article of the Indian Constitution is the executive power of the Union of India formally vested in the President?

options.option_text: Article 74 (which establishes the Council of Ministers)
Article 52 (which establishes the office of the President)
Article 53 (which vests executive power in the President)
Article 75 (which governs the appointment of Prime Minister)

questions.explanation: Article 53(1) explicitly states that the executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President and shall be exercised by him directly or through officers subordinate to him. Article 52 merely creates the office of the President without conferring any power. A common error is conflating Article 52 (establishment) with Article 53 (power-conferral).

questions.stem: Article 75(3) of the Constitution specifies that the Council of Ministers at the Union level is collectively responsible to which body?

options.option_text: The Rajya Sabha as the upper house of Parliament
The Lok Sabha as the popularly elected lower house
The President of India acting as constitutional head
Both Houses of Parliament meeting in a joint session

questions.explanation: Article 75(3) unambiguously provides that the Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People (Lok Sabha). The Rajya Sabha is a common distractor because it represents the Union, but it plays no role in collective responsibility. The President is the constitutional head to whom individual ministers are responsible, but collective responsibility runs to the Lok Sabha alone.

questions.stem: When the Lok Sabha is dissolved before the expiry of its normal term, what is the correct constitutional position of the sitting Council of Ministers?

options.option_text: Ministers continue as caretaker government until new Lok Sabha is formed
Ministers must immediately vacate office when the Lok Sabha is dissolved
The President directly handles all executive functions without ministers
The Rajya Sabha temporarily takes over the dissolved Lok Sabha's duties

questions.explanation: Dissolution of the Lok Sabha does not ipso facto terminate the Council of Ministers. Article 74 mandates that there shall always be a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President, so the outgoing ministry stays on as a caretaker government with limited powers until a new House is constituted and a new government is formed. Ministers immediately vacating office is a constitutional impossibility because the President cannot function without a CoM.

questions.stem: Article 78 of the Constitution imposes a duty on the Prime Minister to communicate to the President which of the following?

options.option_text: Only bills passed by Parliament that require Presidential assent before enactment
Decisions on foreign policy and national security matters exclusively
All Cabinet decisions on Union affairs and proposals for legislation
Only matters where the President has specifically called for information

questions.explanation: Article 78 imposes three duties on the PM: (a) communicate all decisions of the CoM relating to administration of Union affairs and proposals for legislation; (b) furnish information the President may call for; and (c) if the President so requires, place before the CoM any matter decided by a single Minister without Cabinet consideration. The scope in clause (a) is proactive and covers all Cabinet decisions — not merely bills, and not limited to the President's specific requests.

questions.stem: Which category of sentences falls EXCLUSIVELY within the President's pardoning power under Article 72 and is beyond the scope of a Governor's power under Article 161?

options.option_text: Sentences imposed under a state law for heinous criminal offences
Life imprisonment sentences awarded directly by sessions courts
Sentences for contempt of court passed by various High Courts
Sentences awarded by a court-martial or military tribunal

questions.explanation: Article 72(1)(a) specifically empowers the President to grant pardons for sentences inflicted by a court-martial. Article 161, which confers the Governor's pardoning power, contains no such provision — the Governor cannot pardon court-martial sentences at all. This is a PYQ-high-hit distinction. Sentences under State laws (option A) can be pardoned by the Governor; sessions court sentences and contempt sentences are not categorically excluded from the Governor's reach.

questions.stem: In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court's Constitution Bench held that a proclamation imposing President's Rule under Article 356 is:

options.option_text: Justiciable; Presidential satisfaction reviewable if based on irrelevant grounds
Absolutely non-justiciable as it involves pure political discretion only
Valid automatically for 6 months without requiring Parliamentary approval
Challengeable only after both Houses of Parliament approve the proclamation

questions.explanation: The 9-judge bench in S.R. Bommai (1994) overruled the earlier view that Article 356 is wholly non-justiciable. It held that courts can examine whether the President's satisfaction was based on relevant material; if founded on irrelevant, extraneous, or mala fide grounds, the proclamation can be struck down and the dismissed ministry restored. Option B reflects the pre-Bommai position that was definitively rejected. The Court also held that the floor test in the Assembly must precede invoking Article 356.

questions.stem: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 inserted a proviso to Article 74(1) regarding the President's power to return advice. Which of the following correctly states the post-amendment constitutional position?

options.option_text: The President may return advice multiple times and reject it even after reconsideration
The President holds an absolute veto over all executive decisions of Council of Ministers
The President can return advice once, but is bound to act on re-submitted advice
The President can refer any advice to the Supreme Court for advisory opinion first

questions.explanation: The proviso added to Article 74(1) by the 44th Amendment provides that the President may return the advice of the Council of Ministers once for reconsideration, but if the CoM resubmits the same or different advice, the President is constitutionally obligated to act on it. This makes the President's veto merely suspensive — one-time delay, not rejection. Option A (multiple returns) is wrong because the Constitution permits only a single remand. Option B (absolute veto) contradicts the entire parliamentary character of the Constitution, which the Amendment was designed to reinforce after the Emergency experience.
